Chapter 8. The Social Stigma of Poverty.
There's a quiet kind of shame that comes with being poor in America. It's not just about scraping by, trying to make ends meet—it's about how others look at you... and eventually, how you start to see yourself.
The world can be quick to judge, can’t it? There’s this assumption that poverty happens because of laziness, or bad choices. But for the folks actually living through it, that stigma is everywhere.
Imagine a mother standing in line at the grocery store. She’s counting out her dollars and food stamps, hoping she has enough. She can feel the eyes of the cashier, the people waiting behind her—impatience, judgment, all of it. Maybe she wants to explain—to tell them about her job that just doesn’t pay enough, about the rent that keeps climbing, about her kids who need new shoes. But she stays silent. The shame is heavy, and it sticks with her, long after she’s left the store.
At work, the stigma takes on a quieter form. Maybe a coworker cracks a joke about “welfare queens” or “lazy people,” not realizing how close they are themselves to needing help. There’s this fear of being found out, of being seen as "less than." So, people hide their struggles, put on a brave face, and just try to blend in.
The truth is, poverty is isolating. It builds not just financial barriers, but social and emotional ones too. Friendships start to fade, opportunities dry up, and suddenly, the world feels a whole lot smaller. That shame? It seeps in, and over time, it shapes how people see themselves.
But here’s something powerful—there are still moments of defiance. Like when a worker stands up to a supervisor who’s being unfair, or a parent manages to give their child a special birthday, even on a tight budget. These small acts? They’re reminders that dignity can survive, even when times are toughest.
